summary: The District's only frontier-risk action found is AG Brian Schwalb co-signing the Sept 2026 state-AG letter urging federal frontier-AI safety rules, after joining the 2025 anti-preemption letter. No DC Council frontier-AI legislation was found.

items.title: 26-AG letter to Congress on frontier AI safety
items.text: The District of Columbia attorney general signed the letter urging Congress to adopt federal frontier-AI safety rules and to bar preemption of state AI laws.

items.title: 36-AG NAAG letter opposing federal preemption of state AI laws
items.text: The District of Columbia attorney general joined the bipartisan letter urging Congress to reject a moratorium on state AI laws.

profile.headline: Washington, D.C. has a mayoral AI values order that governs how the city government itself uses AI.

sections.text: Mayor Muriel Bowser's Order 2024-028 (February 2024) set six AI values, an 18-month strategic plan and an internal AI Taskforce due to sunset on December 31, 2026. In July 2025 the city piloted deliberation.io, a public-consultation tool from MIT and Stanford, to gather residents' views on AI.

The District hosts no hyperscale AI campuses; the region's large data centers sit in Northern Virginia, mainly Loudoun County (July 2026). DC still shares the PJM grid, so capacity-auction costs driven partly by data-center demand reach Pepco bills. A study commissioned by DC's Office of the People's Counsel (April 2025) estimated the 2025/2026 auction would add about $10 a month, or 9%, to the average residential bill from June 2025.

sources.outlet: DC Office of the People's Counsel / Synapse

sections.text: George Washington University co-leads the $20 million NSF/NIST Institute for Trustworthy AI in Law and Society (TRAILS), and in December 2025 launched a university-wide AI strategy mapping exercise led by Zoe Szajnfarber. Howard University's Human-Centered AI Institute, founded in 2022 and funded by the Office of Naval Research, builds decision-support tools and ran Project Elevate Black Voices, a 600-hour dataset of African American speech.

Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton said at a House Oversight hearing in June 2025 that "AI is a tool that can empower our public servants, but it is not a substitute for passionate and committed federal workers." In August 2026 she introduced a bill to add AmeriCorps positions, citing AI shrinking entry-level jobs. Norton announced her retirement in January 2026; Council member Robert White won the June 2026 Democratic primary to succeed her. No AI statements from White were found.
